utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you are to continue -- or did you finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was a map that we were discussing when we ended, Mr. Tapuskovic, and I'm not sure whether we had settled the issue of its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the question is whether you want to have this map admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, it is not necessary. I think the witness explained certain things concerning that map and we shall not insist on its admittance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would like to tender this map. It's very difficult to read a transcript to which the witness referred to making these thoughts, so I think it should be part of the record as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a little unusual for the Prosecutor to seek to tender a Defence exhibit, but why not? We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood well, and according to the information I have, it wasn't saved at that moment the way it was with all of its markings and some additional markings should have been entered. That's why I expressed our view that we didn't seek its admission. If it is in the form it used to be, then I have nothing against its admittance; but unless all of the markings are there, we need to enter them again. If need be, I can go through it all with the witness again, but I wanted to try and save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to make an issue out of it. If the Defence feels the exhibit doesn't properly reflect what the witness said, then fine, it doesn't need to be tendered from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have already admitted it and we maintain that position. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was previously marked as -- marked for identification as D237, but now it will be admitted as P773.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have another look at the map just to make sure. We don't object it becoming a Defence exhibit, but the way I understood was that it is no longer there, that the markings have been raised. Of course, as Defence counsel, I do not object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if I recall -- if I recall the course of events correctly from last Thursday, the witness put some markings on the Dobrinja map, but then for some reason, for some technical reason, it all disappeared. And then we asked the witness to put the markings back again, and I think this is what now appears on the screen. And I find this map with the witness's markings to have some evidentiary value, so I suggest we just take it as your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we have spent enough time on this. Please commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, I was misinformed. I have nothing against this being admitted as a Defence exhibit. I saw it now, but the way I understood was that it was lost, that it no longer existed. That's why I tried to save time. Of course the witness entered his markings, and since he's our witness this should be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was lost but has been found. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest over the weekend. I don't think it should take too long this morning. I would like to ask you a few questions first about your unit. You remember on Thursday you were asked several questions about your unit, about the weaponry used by your unit, even the weaponry or the armament used by the ABiH. You, I think, were asked a question about what kind of projectiles you heard whizzing past your head in those days. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. There were some ropes or something, I don't know what it's called exactly, but they went across Dobrinja. The lines would fall on to Dobrinja and kids would run out into the street and try to grab the line or the thread. You could hear it whizzing around and see the rips, but in Dobrinja we were safe. It was quite close to the confrontation lines, but still rather quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you first, you told us, you believe, that you were part -- that your company was part of an armoured battalion. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning there was the TO --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovic --

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovic let me just focus on the time of the summer 1994 and into 1995. I think you told us that you were a company quarter-master?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were also in charge or concerned with communications. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on communications and on securing food for the troops. There weren't too many of them, so I was also assigned to be on duty next to the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And that applied to the time after August 1995 and -- after August 1994 and 1995, is that correct, during that time you were quarter-master of your company and at the same time doing communications?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was someone from the logistics. I was a quarter-master of sorts since I was tasked with providing food for the soldiers and also worked with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. The only part I'm now interested in is a time. Is it correct that your function you just described you held sometime from the middle of 1994 and during the whole of 1995. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us again, did your company have a name, have a number?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its name was an infantry company with the armoured battalion, but we were never actually a part of that battalion, or rather, we never left our positions at Dobrinja IV, although we were attached to a higher echelon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the commander of your company, which you told us on Thursday was comprised of about 24, 25 people?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember. It was a long time ago and I'm an elderly man. I don't know what the name was. There were changes all the time. One would arrive and then one would flee or leave the positions and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember the name of another officer, perhaps a captain, perhaps a major, who was part of your company, of your battalion, of your brigade, can you assist us with a couple of names, during that time in 1994 and 1995? It doesn't matter if you don't remember, then you just let me know.

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I'm unable to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to what you also told us on Thursday, that you believe you were part, I think you said, the Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade. Now, I'm curious because we were told by the Defence that you were part of the Ilidza Brigade and that you would testify about the weaponry, about the activities of the Ilidza Brigade, and that's, in fact, what we prepared for. So were you -- was your armed battalion, your company, operating in Dobrinja IV, was that part of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unsure how to explain that. We were a unit in Dobrinja IV, and we were not attached to anyone in particular. We also were not supplied by anyone. Therefore, we asked the municipal president, that is, the president of the Serb municipality of Ilidza, to help us since that was or used to be a part of the Ilidza municipality. They accepted, and they forwarded humanitarian aid on a monthly basis, particularly for the civilians of Dobrinja I and IV. That I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you confident enough to tell us that you were a part of the Ilidza Brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. We didn't belong to anyone in particular. Those up there wouldn't accept us as their own. We were simply the people trying to defend the population of Dobrinja I and IV. Since there were but a few of us, we were assisted by some others, for example, the farmers and citizens who lived there. When there was a skirmish, they would come to lend a hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us on Thursday, and this is on page 6.708, that you heard over your radio that Ilidza had been attacked and shelled and that was in June 1995. What kind of a radio was that, Mr. Jovic? Was that the radio you were listening to as part of your second job, in communications?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some car batteries and we connected the equipment to the batteries. That was the only way to hear anything when we had -- we had small transistors that we could listen the news over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well, I understand. That was a normal, commercial radio, although makeshift, you were listening to that. That was public radio you were listening to, not a military radio system?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- we listened to the public radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The brigade that was around Ilidza, that did also comprise the sector of Nedzarici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep telling you that I never left Dobrinja IV. According to the information I had, there was the TO in Nedzarici. I could hear information now and then on the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of Colonel Vladimir Radojcic, the commander of the Ilidza Brigade? Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave that subject and go on to the situation in Dobrinja. Where was your location as a quarter-master in September 1994? Where was your office or where was your trench or whatever location you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on duty in an apartment of the building. We had no trenches whatsoever. We guarded that part of Dobrinja from the apartments there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think you told us on Thursday that the only thing you could see was Mojmilo hill and the sky above Mojmilo hill. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it, and if I may add, I could also see two large buildings that are in federation territory nowadays, and we feared those two buildings the most, since these are high-rises dominating the entire territory inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also told us on Thursday that you were told not to shoot at civilians. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did that warning or that order apply throughout the period of 1992 until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever it was ordered, no one fired. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just ask you again. That order, not to fire at civilians, did that apply to you in second part of 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, or only in a specific period within that time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, to us, the Orthodox, it wasn't in our interest to destroy civilians. It was in our interest to remain in the parts where we were and to be left alone. We left attacked anyone. I can tell you for sure that no one would open fire on civilians. If one does that, it is an act of genocide, in my terms, it is a crime, a horrible crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was it that ordered you not to shoot civilians? Can you tell Their Honours a specific individual? Do you remember anybody who told you that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be conveyed orders by the officer on duty, that person would usually introduce themselves, and they would say that the orders are not to fire in any circumstances. And if someone fired and they would be able to hear it, then on occasion they would call and say, Who's the fool who fired and why? But as far as I know, none of our soldiers ever fired. There were some people who assisted us on occasion in Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, Mr. Jovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- counsel had asked you whether the order not to fire at civilians applied in the second part of 1992, all of 1993, all of 1994, and 1995. He wanted to know whether the order not to fire applied from 1992 to 1995, but you didn't answer that question directly. What is the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a standing order from the beginning of the war not to fire on the population and for no reason. It was there in 1992, 1993, and especially in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Dobrinja, it was calm throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you told us that the officer on duty, the duty officer, conveyed the orders to you not to shoot at civilians. Do you remember the name or the rank at least of this duty officer?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know? I never left Dobrinja IV. I could only hear a voice over the telephone, and it was a line going directly to the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why was it a repetitive order if, as you say, you never were shooting at civilians? Why did it have to be repeated throughout the time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When fire was opened from the other side targeting us, then there would be a reply, so they kept calling. As soon as they would hear fire from our positions, they would call us and tell us, Don't fire, don't respond to any provocations. It often happened. There was a sniper shooting at civilians and, for example, that shooter would wound or kill a civilian, and in order for us to be able to reach that civilian we had to target the sniper in order to pull that person out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying that the ABiH used snipers to target civilians on your side? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, I saw a sniper, I saw that rifle. People often referred to it as a sniping rifle, but it may have been an ordinary rifle, too, because there was not more than 100 metres between the confrontation lines. It sufficed that someone stuck his head out, or if there was a woman or a child, to get shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, please attend to the question which is being asked, and the question was whether you're saying that the ABiH used snipers to target civilians on your side. Never mind the characteristics of the rifle. Are you saying that the ABiH used snipers to target civilians on your side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe they did, and I didn't see that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovic. But there were civilians living on the ABiH-controlled side of Dobrinja, for instance, in Dobrinja II and III. That's correct, Mr. Jovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And very much like you, these people had to go into the outside to get food, to get water. Isn't that correct, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On Thursday in the first time you looked at this SFOR map you circled a church, I think that was the Orthodox church, and you marked it with a C. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this Orthodox church, the Serbian Orthodox church, was a very, very good observation point from which you could observe the whole of Dobrinja. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in that church nor could I come close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But there were people from your side, perhaps these people, you had explained a moment ago who came to assist your company, who were occupying that Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never occupied the Orthodox church. As far as I know, I even made a contribution when that church was being built. There was no need to occupy it when it was on Serb-held territory. It was on territory occupied by Orthodox people -- I mean where Orthodox people lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jovic, you and your unit, whether it was your company, whether it was the armed battalion in that area, were defending that part of the line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja IV, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why would you not use such a fantastic vantage point like the Orthodox church provided you with?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was in Dobrinja IV and the church was a bit further away from Dobrinja IV. I was looking after my family and the families of the people who were with me. I was not interested in what they were doing on the other side. Our aim was only to prevent slaughter of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. My question was more towards the people who were a part of your battalion, and I said that there might be people part of your battalion who were sitting, observing, perhaps shooting from those excellent positions on the Serbian Orthodox church. Do you have any knowledge about people occupying positions on the Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was abandoned, but quite honestly I don't know the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just go back to what you told us a minute ago, and I already referred to that as well. You told us that there were some people who assisted us in the defence of Dobrinja, and this is on page 10, lines 14 to 16. Who were these people who came to assist you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were men from the rear, cooks and the inhabitants of the suburban villages, the villages near the town, who had their families in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Thursday as well that you were the, I think, local president of Dobrinja. Do you remember that? The president of the local commune, and this is on page 6712.

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I take it you knew and still know Dobrinja fairly well, not just the Serb parts at that time, Dobrinja IV and I, but also Dobrinja II and III. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of Dobrinja I, and so I knew that area quite well. But I didn't know the neighbouring areas so well. Everybody had his own local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you are familiar with the river Dobrinja that was in the middle of Dobrinja II and Dobrinja III?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to positions at Dobrinja IV, and I saw that river flowing through Indira Gandhi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So from your positions at Dobrinja IV, you could see the River Dobrinja flowing through?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you're familiar with the fact that there were bridges over the River Dobrinja, connecting Dobrinja II and Dobrinja III within ABiH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see that from the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us also on Thursday that you could not believe that snipers would target a girl or a woman. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, have you heard that on 6th of January, 1994, a woman aged 32 who was riding on her bicycle was shot at when crossing one of the bridges between Dobrinja II and III, and it was determined that the shots originated from the Orthodox church, the Serbian Orthodox church? Did you hear of that at that time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you hear of other incidents, and I just give you one example. On 11th of July, when a 48-year woman was killed, again in ABiH-held territory, just at the Dobrinja part facing you and she was killed when fetching water from the Dobrinja water -- from the Dobrinja River. Have you heard of that example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, only the 11th of July was mentioned but no year was mentioned. We don't know what year that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I thought I said it, but I'm happy to repeat. It's 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 11th July 1993. You haven't heard about the killing of a 40-year-old [sic] woman who was trying to fetch water in the Dobrinja -- at the Dobrinja River? You haven't heard about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also told us, Mr. Jovic, that occasionally you would go out and stretch your legs and play football. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, your colleagues on the other side did the same, they also wanted to stretch their legs and play football. Have you heard that on the 1st of June, 1993, there was a makeshift football game organised in Dobrinja III B on the parking lot only a few hundred metres opposite where your positions were; and two 82-millimetre mortar shells were launched on to a large crowd, perhaps about 200 people, including numerous civilians, and there were casualties. And the shots were determined to come from SRK-held territory. Have you heard about that, 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I'm truly sorry if this happened, but I don't know who could have done that and why. I don't know where it could have been fired from. Perhaps it was a stray projectile. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And have you heard that in June 1995 the Simon Bolivar school, to which you referred to on Thursday as well, was shelled, causing casualties among civilians who were queuing for water? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember on the federation television they said something about that, and to tell you quite sincerely, I am sorry for all the victims. I am sorry about my family but also about all the others on the other side, too. I'm sorry there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, that concludes your evidence; thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, may I say something to this Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not customary, Mr. Jovic. You have given your evidence and that is what you came here for, so you may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness? The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Mr. Branislav Dukic, and I believe he's ready. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell the Court your full name?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branislav Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you this, but I would like to repeat it. Please look at the transcript appearing before you, and when you see the end of my question, when words stop appearing on the screen, only then please begin to answer my question. You were born on the 7th of September, 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Petrovski, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The secondary technical school in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The faculty of work organisation in 1987, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you've been living in Sarajevo since 1965?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours where you worked, where you were employed, and in what part of Sarajevo this was.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a special honour to be here before you today. I have not come to defend General Dragoljub [as interpreted] Milosevic, but to tell you my truth as I experienced it in Sarajevo. I was not a member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are to answer the questions asked by counsel. Just attend to the questions which he asks and answer them. Don't volunteer any statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a member --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, please. Just answer my questions. This is very important, please. Just tell us what you experienced yourself. The Court is interested only in what you saw and experienced, so I'm asking you, first of all, where were you employed and where you lived.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I worked in Famos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please wait for my question to appear on the monitor and then start your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I worked in Famos. I lived in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you live in Hrasnica and since when have you been working in Famos?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I've been working in Famos since 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you live with your family and who were your family members?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I lived in the Partiranska Street 2B in Hrasnica. I had a wife and a son. I lived with my wife and son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now please explain to the Judges what happens, or rather, what happened in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: As I said at the outset, that I was not a member of any political party, I did not want to leave Sarajevo. I remained with my family, my wife and my son. But before that, in March, I was called-up by the TO, the Territorial Defence of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get call-up papers from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I did not accept this call-up, and I did not want to carry a gun, a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992, Samir Agic, a neighbour of my mine, and three other men entered my flat, fired shots from a Kalashnikov in the hallway of the building. They arrested me and they handcuffed me with plastic handcuffs. My son was only 13. They locked him in the bathroom. My wife lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anybody killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, not on that day, no. They took me to the Aleksa Santic primary school. When I arrived there, I saw between 25 and 30 men in the lobby of the primary school. We spent three or four hours there. We were surrounded by armed men, armed with light weapons. And after a few hours they took us toward the football stadium belonging to the Famos football club. There were wooden and iron bars on the outside. They put us there. There were guards there, people with light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did you stay there? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: We spent only a few hours there. Then they took us back to the primary school, the Aleksa Santic primary school, where I found another group of ten Serbs who had been brought in. Ratko Stjepanovic was among them, and he cursed their Muslim mother. Then they shot him, they killed him, in that primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw this happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for five or six days. We had some sort of blankets. A few days later Amir Sabovic arrived, I know him personally, these are all people from Famos. They introduced him as a police commander. When Mr. Sabovic saw me and some others he knew, he asked that we be released and allowed to go home. Unfortunately, those were Juka Prazina's Green Berets and there was some sort of trouble among them. And we learned a few days later that Amir Sabovic had been dismissed from the post of police commander. We were taken from that primary school to a residential building, we were taken to the basement there. They threw in a few blankets and a few boards for us to make beds for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you be very brief and just tell us the most important points, because we have very little time. So we cannot tell the Court about everything you saw and experienced.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: There were 51 of us in our group, and they immediately gave us picks and shovels. And we set out towards the source of the River Bosna, where Tito's villa used to be. That place is called Stojcevac. I had a pick and comrade of mine had a shovel, and in one day we had to dig 2 and a half metres in length and 1 and a half metres in width. We were digging trenches. This went on for days and days. After that, we went towards Bojkovici, and then to Igman to dig dug-outs and trenches, as well as trenches for 120-millimetre mortars. When I say that, I'm a reserve officer so I'm familiar with different types of weapons. We would spend as much as a month there sleeping in tents right next to the front lines and their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what happened? Was there any shooting, firing, from either side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, at the very beginning, there was no shooting; but in 1993, that was hell for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir. In 1993 -- you'll tell us what happened, but what happened in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, on the 4th of August, 1992, the Muslim forces attacked Famos and there were big battles. There were heavy losses on the Muslim side. Around 1700 hours in the afternoon, they took a group of 51 of us, our group, and they used us as a human shield in order to pull out their dead. When we arrived at the front line, when we looked towards Lasica, the area between Lasica and Famos, we saw that there were women and children there holding hands to terrify people and to prevent a counter-offensive by the Serb forces. Then I saw my 13-year-old son in that group of women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. The witness said he could clearly make a difference between a 120-millimetre mortar and other weapons because he was a reserve officer. In French I heard this translated as "officier de reserve" but this I think leads to some confusion because "officier de reserve" in French means somebody who has the rank of a commander. Because "officier de reserve" in French could be a simple rank-and-file soldier. Could the witness kindly tell me what exactly was his rank at the time when he was reserve officer and which his specialisation was, or what he was specialised in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait. Judge Mindua wanted to know something. Can you explain to the Court how come you had that rank and in what time, when was it that you were with the reserve.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: You know that I served my military term with the JNA. Once I completed the university, usually such people went to attend a reserve officer's school. After that I was awarded the rank of a lieutenant, 2nd lieutenant, and we were taught in manoeuvre operations at peacetime, after which I received the rank of a lieutenant. After that training, I no longer attended exercises of the reserve force and I remained a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you had no further dealings with the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No. We were all there, ready to be mobilised, as any other soldier. The only difference was that we with the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So did you have any special training in handling of arms, because you mentioned a 120-millimetre mortar? In other words, what was your field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked with 120-millimetre mortars. I was with the artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After completing university, you were with the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 18th of April and until the end of the war, what were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I was a prisoner, digging trenches. I was exchanged on the 20th of January, 1995, as part of the exchange organised by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what ensued after April. What was happening during the time you were digging those trenches? Can you tell us the highlights?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: As I said, we were digging trenches all the time. We started from Stojcevac in Igman towards Vojkovici, Ilidza, Butmir, and in 1993 we were forced to dig a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were digging a tunnel, but before that while you were digging trenches, what was happening with the people who were doing that and what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Quite often certain people could not stand the psychological abuse and the daily physical labour. Some of them tried to flee to the other side, and then they would be killed. It happened that in a single month, two or three of them were killed, those of us who were digging trenches. We were always at the front line, and sometimes one couldn't really know who was it that killed that person, whether it was a shell that landed or someone fired directly at that person. We didn't know exactly where we were and how things stood. We were abused by people we didn't know. On the other hand, the people that we knew did not want to stand up for us and, in a way, they tried to steer clear of such situations. Those who abused us were always people we didn't know. May I add something else? There were people who would start fleeing through the woods and come across a land-mine or a field of mines. I know of such a case of a man who was inside a minefield for three months and no one could pull him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the mortars that you can -- recognised from some previous times. Did you have anything to do with such mortars and what did that look like?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Since we were with the troops non-stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Since we were with the soldiers at the front line all the time, when they would be discovered by the Serb side, when the Serb side would reveal their mortar positions, then what would ensue would be a command to move the mortars to another position. And we would have to dig day and night, making dug-outs and the rest at the new position, and then together with the troops we were also supposed to transport ammunition and the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many mortars were there in Hrasnica, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Since I'm an artillery man, according to my military specialty, I can tell you that an artillery battery comprises six mortars. There were three times six of such mortars, that is, 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I'm not completely sure, but I don't recall the witness saying there were mortars in Hrasnica; and if indeed he did not say that, then my submission would be that the question is leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say in Hrasnica, I said at Igman. Igman is a mountain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said"Hrasnica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslim positions were up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Avoid leading questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hrasnica is a town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Avoid leading questions, Mr. Tapuskovic. How much longer will you be with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been given one hour. I began half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking for that reason. It's because at the end of your examination-in-chief I'm going to ask you to identify the particular relevance of this evidence to the indictment. Go ahead, but prepare yourself for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I was expecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell me directly, please, while you were at the positions doing all the things you did, such as digging, for how long did you stay in the prison? Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I was in Hrasnica in prison until the 5th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as a matter of fact, I'd like you to do that right now, to say to us how this witness's evidence, the evidence that he's given thus far, assists you in the defence of the accused, who is charged with terror, who is charged with crimes against humanity, and certain other offences in breach of the Geneva Conventions. He has given evidence which may very well be credible of how the Serbs suffered at the hands of the ABiH. Now, tell us how this particular evidence relates to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness's testimony will help you establish how many imprisoned Serbs were there and as well as people of other ethnicities and how many of them were killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you need to establish how many imprisoned Serbs there were? What -- how is that relevant to any of the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It proves that terror suffered by the Serb population in the part of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is proof that this man, as well as some others - and I will bring another two witnesses who will testify to that - that all this was unnecessary, the suffering they underwent, and because of which, particularly towards the end of the war, the people had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what if it was unnecessary? The accused is charged with certain crimes, you know, and what this gentleman is saying that the Serbs suffered. I don't understand the Prosecution to be contesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only motive during the relevant period and other periods due to which people stayed at their positions, the positioned discussed here, was because they wanted to avoid the fate, such as mentioned here, to -- not to have to undergo the treatment this man suffered. They tried to flee to the other side, and the people on the other side, the Serb side of the line, tried to save their lives and to defend themselves. During the period of the indictment, such people were only concerned with staying at the positions so as not to be exposed to the treatment suffered by this and other men in the hands of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were -- there were 126 prisons in the ABiH territory. The suffering people saw was what kept them in the trenches and at the front lines, because they did not want to suffer the same fate. In the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, such things did not occur. The terror mentioned here, especially during the period of the indictment, actually existed but it was inflicted upon the Serb population in the part of Sarajevo controlled by the ABiH and not at Grbavic, Nedzarici, or the other parts that was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were hundreds killed -- people killed while digging trenches. Things like that were the main motive of the people to defend their homes, and of course they had to reply to such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So far the most relevant point that you have made is that the terror that was inflicted during the period of the indictment actually existed, but it was inflicted on the Serb population in the area controlled by the ABiH and not at Grbavica and Nedzarici. So you're saying that the terror that is charged in the indictment is not attributable to the accused and the Serbs but to the ABiH. Is that how you're seeking to answer the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will provide an answer to your question. At this moment, I still don't know what the scope of things that the Prosecutor is trying to prove is. I'm trying to deal with certain facts that may here be seen as adjudicated facts. This is why I keep stressing the importance of these issues. On the other hand, I never contested that the combat activities at that time were something that inflicted suffering upon both peoples. I do not dare do that and I am certainly not allowed to. But to state that the only goal of the Army of Republika Srpska was to terrorise inhabitants, particularly during the relevant time, is completely out of place. During the period referred to in the indictment with a view of everything that was taking place and with a view of things that this witness was testifying to was the main reason why the people on the Serb side remained at their positions. They simply did not want to meet the fate met by this and other people. Of course there was suffering on both sides because of the military activities. I just wanted to show that inflicting suffering and terrorising the population on the other side of the line was not the goal of the Serb army. The true terror, literally speaking, existed within the area of responsibility of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war. The same situation did not exist within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps when we count the number of human lives and people killed outside combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, I want to submit that the Prosecution's position is that not that the accused terrorised -- that the only goal of the VRS was to terrorise the civilian population in Sarajevo but that it was the primary purpose. And therefore, we're not required to prove that it was the only purpose, the VRS activity in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just about to read that from the indictment, in fact, from Articles 51, paragraph 2, of Additional Protocol I, and Article 32 of Additional Protocol II. "Acts or threats of violence, the primary purpose of which is to spread terror among the civilian population are prohibited," but then I would imagine Mr. Tapuskovic is -- would be saying that that is not established, you know, you have not established that the primary purpose of such acts of violence or threats of violence as there were was to spread terror and that any terror that existed was incidental to the acts or threats of violence, which are a normal part of any war. So that may be his case, but I still have difficulty detecting the linkage, the tie, between this evidence and that broad proposition. It must be that what you are saying is that any terror that existed was, in fact, caused by the ABiH, the acts of violence of the ABiH, not the Serb army. And any that was caused by the Serb army would not amount to being the primary purpose of those acts or threats of violence. I'll consult my colleagues on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in the circumstances, we are allowing you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for the speed with which I speak because of course then the interpreters cannot interpret everything I say. So I will try to say a few sentences in three or four minutes to clarify my position. Because I am hurrying, I am sometimes unable to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's get on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- explain things in the right sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to expedite matters, while you were imprisoned - and you've already explained what happened - how many people who were prisoners were killed in the course of the time up to 1994 that you were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I said until the 9th of September, 1994, I was in Hrasnica. As there was no Orthodox cemetery or Serbian cemetery in Hrasnica, 96 men were killed, including three or four children, and a new cemetery was created near the old primary school at the entrance to Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But how were these people killed? Can you give at least a few examples of people you knew?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, at the outset, I already said that some were killed while trying to escape, others were killed even in their own homes. Some were killed while digging, and those were the ones we buried; and to identify them we secretly put their first and last names on the corpse. I don't want to assert anything, but when I was exchanged I learned that in Hrasnica there were 126 graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the tunnel. What can you tell us about the tunnel? What did this look like and did you have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In 1993 work on digging a tunnel under the Butmir runway began from the Butmir side. As I've already said that we dug towards Ilidza, Butmir, and Vukovici, we prisoners were taken to dig those tunnels as needed when we had to dig other lines we would then be transferred to Igman to dig more trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But what did the digging of the tunnel look like from your side, were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: When we started digging, we started from an old house, and then we had to break through the basement and three men were killed digging the tunnel; because they were so weak and exhausted that they could no longer dig, and this would give rise to an argument and then they would be killed, murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was a relative of mine, Stevo Dukic, and I could list many others but let me mention just his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in prison in that place, did anyone visit you and inquire about the fate of those men?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we knew that the International Committee of the Red Cross was coming to Hrasnica, and we managed to speak to some people from SFOR asking for help. But unfortunately they did not help us. The International Committee of the Red Cross was unable to find us because they would hide us, they would conceal us, moving us from one location to another when they learned that the ICRC was about to pay a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you're more observant than I am. Yes, it is time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were there from April 1992 to September 1994?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us throughout this time who did you observe in the area. If you could first explain to Their Honours what Hrasnica actually is. Where is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica was a part of Sarajevo, a part of Ilidza municipality, which was part of the city of Sarajevo. The population of Hrasnica was about 70 per cent Muslim and about 30 per cent Serb and Croat. The Muslim forces going out went via Hrasnica, Igman, Turcin, and on towards Croatia. That was their main route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the tunnel you worked on was finished and how it was used?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The tunnel was large enough for two people to pass by each other, and there was a small railway track there for a small train which could be used to carry goods. We even loaded crates of ammunition passing through the tunnel on that little train.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you say it was mostly Muslim, Serb, and Croats who lived there, but while you were there who did you see there most often?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I know that when we were digging at Igman we also maintained the so-called white road. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Ejub Ganic, and many other public figures would come by from the fields of politics, culture, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not really what I wanted to ask, but since you said that did these people see you there? Did they know who you were?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they knew. I won't go into it now, but I know that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a document where Alija Izetbegovic says that Hrasnica and the other camps are camps for those held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But can you answer my question: Who did you see there most often?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin also came via Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question either, but since you've mentioned it now, go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Mujahedin would come by way of Igman and pass through on their way to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation at the time with respect to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards the civilian population, the Serbs did nothing but dig and work and there was no way they could go over to the free territory. They were simply hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned mortars. Was there any fighting, any firing, and were you able to observe that? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was firing. I told you we were with the army all the time at the positions, and of course they fired from mortars, from small-arms, and everything else that they had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they were firing at what?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in the direction of Ilidza, Hadzici, Vojkovici, and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until November, when I was transferred through the tunnel to the Viktor Bubanj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the Viktor Bubanj barracks was?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: May I describe how we went through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: When they brought me and three others, because they transferred us in groups, I was in the first group with three others. And when we entered the tunnel, there were over 200 soldiers there waiting to pass through. And when we arrived at the tunnel, they blindfolded us with a white bandage. And then there was panic because they said, Are those Chetniks you've taken prison? And they started hitting us with whatever they -- came to hand. And someone even fired shots to calm those people down, because we would simply have been killed by the soldiers, but there were also civilians there among them. When we were passing through the tunnel on our way to Dobrinja we were met by another group, one of them even asked to cut off my ear. Of course they didn't let him do that. They put us into a van and took us to the Dobrinja police station. In Dobrinja we stayed for about an hour there, and then we were taken to the Viktor Bubanj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the Viktor Bubanj barracks and what is it now?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The Viktor Bubanj barracks was a camp for Serbs, and on the third -- on the second and third floors, that was where their army had its quarters. When we entered the Viktor Bubanj barracks they broke my ribs, and I can show it to you if need be, you can see it quite well. Then they knocked out my front teeth and I was in a sorry state, and one of them approached me and stuck a knife point into my eye, here where you can see a scar. And when another guard told him not to do that, he said, Let me beat the Chetnik. When I was able to beat my Alija in the prison in Foca, my president, why wouldn't I be able to beat a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there some kind of international control, a monitoring?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of November of that year, the International Committee of the Red Cross entered. There was a French woman there who registered me and gave me a number, and then she told me, You have survived and now you are under our control. And they visited us every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any proceedings instigated against you after almost two and a half years?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, just before our trial, I was given an indictment, saying that I avoided conscription, that I evaded the call-up, and Alija Izetbegovic, Sulejman Ceric, and Jovan Divjak arrived in the barracks. They entered my cell, cell number 1, and I had to introduce myself when the guards opened the cell door. Much later I saw Mr. Divjak who visited on several occasions. And when he saw my eye, which was all swollen because of the knife prick, they were taking me to the other side of the barracks where the outpatients' clinic was. He saw that I was handcuffed, and so he probably assumed I was a Serb, but he did not react.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you taken before any judges?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a judge there, Amir Jaganjac as well as Miso Salem. When I was brought in handcuffed, he asked that I stay handcuffed by saying that, Chetniks are dangerous, even when tied up, let alone with their hands free. There was also Idriz Kamenica there and Marko Mikerevic as a judge juror. The note-taker was Almasa Mumanagic [phoen], if I remember correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did the proceedings look like, was there a judgement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all sentenced to two years in prison, and after having heard the sentence, my then-counsel who was appointed to me, her name was Senka Nozica, stayed there. And then after that we were transferred to the central prison where I was taken to the cell number 79, that was a central prison in Sarajevo. I was maltreated there as well by the guards there who wouldn't allow me to eat properly. In January 1995 through the mediation of the ICRC, we were exchanged. They came in some armoured vehicles and we were exchanged at the Brdstvo-Jedinstvo bridge. Upon my arrival to Ljubica I met General Dragomir Milosevic. The 52 of us were in an open area. He came by and said, Take those people away from this open aware because a shell will land and they will all be dead. Before that I did not know him and I haven't seen him since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I just wanted to clarify the witness's explanation of the trial against him. Do you understand me, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You said that you were tried and -- by judges, and that you eventually were sentenced to two years' imprisonment. And my question is: What were you charged with? What was the offence that you had allegedly committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dodging a draft, dodging a military service. I -- the president of the Republika Srpska Association of Prisoners. I was at this tribunal before. I met Ms. Carla del Ponte three times, and we submitted all of the documentation we had to her. As concerns your question, she asked me the very same thing. I handed her my indictment because I was given it by the ICRC. She shrugged her shoulders. It reads, Dodging a military draft. At the beginning I said that this was not my war and I did not want to bear arms. I did not want such a war to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Dodging military service because there had been a call-up for everybody living in Hrasnica to join the ABiH, was that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But at that time you had already been imprisoned for quite a long time, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In March, they had been mobilising people. I was taken prisoner on the 18th of April. In March, I refused to accept the draft call and to report for duty. I believed that their army was illegal. These were merely civilians, criminals in my terms, people taking -- taken out of prisons. Some people told me that, but the rumour had it on the Muslim -- among the Muslims and the Croats that prisoners were released from jails.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To establish a link between my examination and the questions posed by Judge Harhoff, I wanted to ask you this: You were not tried on the 18th of April, 1992, rather, you were tried in 1995, a few years later, charging you with the crime?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The trial took place in 1994. As I said, many Serbs went missing and we didn't know where they are. There was no court in Hrasnica or anything else. They were trying to hide us from the ICRC and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that you were tried a short time before you were released?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I guess they knew why. Maybe they knew that there was to be an end to the war soon. The only thing I know that we were tried then in Sarajevo at the Viktor Bubanj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you met Carla del Ponte, did you hand over any documentation concerning the camps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at DD003786, please. Your Honours, upon my request, I received from the Prosecutor for the first time this document, and it makes a whole lot of things clearer, especially certain things that I tried to put through certain witnesses. But at the time when they were here, I didn't have this documentation and these were Prosecutor's witnesses. I don't have it translated. I've only received it very recently, upon my request, and I will try to translate it as soon as possible. Could we for the time being have a look at this document and to tell us what and when he handed over to Carla del Ponte personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When she came to Banja Luka, she heard of our association, of the Republika Srpska Association of Prisoners, and she asked to meet us. There was a meeting which lasted for two hours in Banja Luka. A month later, the same delegation from The Hague Tribunal invited us to come to The Hague, to the Tribunal. We stayed here on a two-day visit, on the 31st of May, 2004, it was. She took the documentation at that time and signed a receipt. What she wanted to gain was access to documentation about civilian casualties primarily because they -- there were casualties among the civilians the most, among the Serbs who remained in Sarajevo and the documentation pertains to that. After that, Carla del Ponte again came to Banja Luka and again asked to meet us. And on that occasion, we also handed over some documentation. The cooperation is still ongoing, either she or people from her team regularly come to Banja Luka or other places in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the signature that Ms. Carla del Ponte affixed to the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the first page so as to be able to see what the date is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see what the date is, and please look at item 11.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it concerns Sarajevo. The plight of the Serbs in Dobrinja, Novi Grad municipality, Pofalici, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: On the list that you handed over, how many camps were listed and how many Serbs went through such camps?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: According to the numbers we have for Sarajevo and the number of people there, there were 126 camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. It is the part of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were around 18.000 -- 17.000 people, camp detainees, and 90 per cent of which were civilians. I also wanted to say this, we have information that around 5.000 people, detainees, came through the Viktor Bubanj barracks. For the most part these were civilians arrested in 1992 at the very beginning of the war. Unfortunately, many of them were not tried and many never left the camp alive, the barracks of Viktor Bubanj. Even today we are still looking for some of them. Another important thing is that we told or asked Ms. Carla del Ponte to react. There is a court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in place there now. She tried to prevent the opening of such a court in that very building since it used to be a camp, but it was too late for her to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During such trials, what sort of guilt were the detainees asked to state their position on?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This document, DD003786 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could it be admitted as a Defence exhibit, since we will also want to use it further with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on the grounds of relevance. The document, the receipt, also speaks to areas that are not -- that are outside Sarajevo, the event of Visegrad, Mrkonjic Grad, for example, and despite my learned friend's submissions this morning, the Prosecution's position is that the alleged suffering of Bosnian Serbs inside Sarajevo has no impact on the charges the accused is charged for. And -- unless of course it's the Defence's position that this serves a motive for the general in the VRS actions. But I don't see the -- I don't see how this document is probative to the charges against the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you take the position, Mr. Sachdeva, that the suffering of the Serbs inside Bosnia-Herzegovina has no impact on the charges in the indictment, then you would have to object to all of the evidence, all of this witness's evidence, because this is what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was -- I had planned to at some point make an objection on that ground, but then, Mr. President, your question, in my submission, required the Defence to explain their position. And in the Prosecution's position, we still don't agree that this evidence of this witness is relevant to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anything in reply, Mr. Tapuskovic? The Prosecutor says this particular item that you're seeking to have exhibited is not relevant. For one, he says, as I understand him, that it deals with an area outside Sarajevo. What do you say to his submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all of a sudden Hrasnica seems to be outside Sarajevo, whereas until now we've been listening about different things done in Hrasnica. And now for the first time we hear from the Prosecutor that Hrasnica is not a part of Sarajevo. That was the first thing. The second thing, although I'm short of time, in item 11 there is mention not of Mrkonjic Grad, as the Prosecutor stated, but it mentions Sarajevo and Dobrinja. Could we move into closed session for a moment so that I can explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Closed session -- well, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received this for the first time --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, I should say that at the beginning of tomorrow's session, which is in the afternoon, I will spend about half an hour considering this question of relevance. I will outline the issue, which is a burning issue for me and for my colleagues as well, and I'll hear from both the Defence and the Prosecutor on it. It's an issue that is a recurring decimal in the -- it's a recurring theme in the Defence case. And I would just like to have a general discussion to hear submissions, legal submissions, on it tomorrow, for no more than 20 minutes. That's at tomorrow's session in the afternoon, the first 20, 25 minutes. Yes, continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dukic, my name is Manoj Sachdeva, and I am a lawyer for the Prosecution, and I am going to be asking you a few questions today.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Good day to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I just start by confirming that your evidence is that you were detained from April 1992 through to September 1994 in Hrasnica. Is that -- am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say "detained," by that I take it you mean that your liberty was taken away from you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your evidence is that you were kept in camps during that period, which is over a year?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But it's right, is it not, that when you went to the trenches you returned and went back to your house during that period in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No. We had premises in a residential building, and we would spend up to a month in the woods at Igman at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So let me just try and understand you. Are you saying that during period from April 1992 through to September 1994, you were not able to spend the night and the evenings at your house in Hrasnica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would let people go and see their families for a day, but otherwise we were all in those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in that period from April 1992 through to September 1994, how many days were you at your house; in other words, at your house in Hrasnica with your family?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Only twice, because my family left. If -- if need be, I can explain how they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to -- I want to get the information about when you went home. I want to understand that. So your evidence is that you went home twice in that period, and for those times you spent one night at home. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: When I said "twice," I meant twice. I asked to go and have a bath.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you meant twice, but what I'm asking you is was that twice for a week, two weeks; or was that twice for just a night; or was that twice for three months, four months. If I understand you you're saying you went home twice and you spent one night in your house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, you gave a statement to the court in Banja Luka, did you not, on March -- in March 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this was roughly one and a half months after you were released in Sarajevo in January 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in March 1995, it's correct that the events that you experienced in Sarajevo were fresh in your mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And presumably when you gave that statement to the court in Banja Luka, you would have included every small detail that you thought was important for the court to hear about your time and detention in Sarajevo. That's also right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: They asked that of me. I didn't explain here all the things that went on, but in the cell when digging trenches, I think there are some things here. The team that interviewed me would go on asking questions and would find out all the things that went on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that I understand, but at least --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do know that it says here that they urinated all over us and things like that. I didn't say that here now but it's in those statements; because they came from The Hague Tribunal and asked about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think perhaps we're not understanding each other. I'm not talking about a statement you gave to the ICTY, which you did give a statement to. I'm talking about the statement you gave in front of the Banja Luka court in March 1995. You understand that I'm talking about that statement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No. I only know about a statement I gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
