utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, let me start again. You gave a statement to the lower court in Banja Luka in March 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that is the statement I'm speaking about at the moment. I will move on to the statement you gave to the ICTY in a moment. And again, what I want to ask you is that when you gave that statement to the court -- to the lower court in Banja Luka, you gave information that you knew to be correct and accurate. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that statement so well. It was probably all fresh in my memory then. How relevant it is and the -- how competent the judges were to take that statement, I don't know, but I do abide by everything I said to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, as I understand it, you're saying that when you gave a statement to the court in Banja Luka, as you said the events were probably all fresh in your memory, you understand what you were telling the court was correct and it was the truth in your mind. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, certain moments, certain events, are still fresh in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's concentrate on the statement in Banja Luka. When you gave that statement in front of the court, you were obliged to tell the truth, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were also warned of the consequences of giving false testimony when you were giving that statement to the lower court. Isn't that also right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: They took that when we left the camps. Those were not judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: These were people who took statements from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I still think that we have a problem of understanding each other, and I'm going to try again. In March 1995 did you or did you not give a statement before the lower court in Banja Luka in front of a judge called Djordje Stojakovic, you remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you did not give a statement to the lower court in Banja Luka? Are you saying that that did not happen at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that person. I don't remember any judge taking a statement from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can assist in trying to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask for 65 ter 03289 to be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, is my signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to show it to you now. Now, Mr. Dukic, you -- you can see that this is entitled "Record of Witness Interview." You can see that, can't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you can see the name of the judge there, Djordje Stojakovic, you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know either him or Jagoda Borojevic, the name that's mentioned here, and Andrej Djordjevic Stojakovic. I don't know who these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You see your name, Branislav Dukic, that's your name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we go to the end of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So now you remember you gave a statement to the lower court in Banja Luka, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that person, Djordje Stojakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the judge, I'm not asking you about the clerk, I'm asking you, as you've confirmed now, that that is your signature. And I take it if that is your signature, you gave a statement to the lower court in Banja Luka. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also agree that as you -- when you gave that statement to the lower court, you were under an obligation to tell the truth and to recall the events as accurately as possible --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in March 1995 it would have been easier for you to remember the events in Sarajevo, because they were fresh in your mind, weren't they, as you've already told the Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to point to a particular topic in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could move to page -- it's page 4 of the English, and I -- I think it's page 4 of the B/C/S. Actually, I think it's page 3, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Dukic, the -- you see the first paragraph on your screen on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And -- and I want to concentrate at a part that is in the middle of that paragraph where it says -- where you have told the court: "In March 1995 I stayed at home for three months." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning I said that they were taking us towards the Famos stadium and the Aleksa Santic school where they mistreated us. After that they didn't mistreat us but they gave us picks and shovels and took us with them to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not actually asking that. What I'm trying to understand from you is that you have told the Court here under oath that you went home only twice in the period April 1992 through to September 1994 and in this statement that you gave in March 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Your evidence is that you were detained from April 1992 through to September 1994, that's --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In this statement that you gave to the court in Banja Luka, you have told the court that you spent three months at your house in Hrasnica. And I'm trying to understand what is correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see where that is. I don't see where it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I was asking whether the interpreter is able to point to the passage in the B/C/S. In the English it's the seventh line in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think in the B/C/S it starts by saying: [B/C/S spoken]; do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can show the witness where that is. It's on page 3, the sentence before the last, but let him read the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that every day the military police, the Green Berets, came, and it says that for three months I was there and then I went -- but it was they who took me to work and brought me back. That was what was meant probably, not that I stayed there. I don't know how they understood this and wrote it down. You see it says here the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you or did you not spend three months in your house, in Hrasnica? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, I did not. Because they came to get me. They took me to work. They brought me back, and they let me see my family when I needed to until they left, but I was accompanied or escorted by the military police or somebody else, and the way they phrased this, I don't know how they did that, how they formulated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To dig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To dig, and from where did they take you? They took you from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To begin with, when they took us back from the stadium and to the school, before they created those rooms in the residential building they would take us home and bring us back or when we needed a bath --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did that happen every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The -- it would happen in the course of the first three months, because there was nowhere for us to take a bath. They still hadn't made the showers and everything else in those basements, in those residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So where did you spend those three months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a time I was at home and for a time I was in those premises, and they would take us to dig with the army for 15 days at a time, living in tents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And for what period were you in those premises? For how long did you remain in those premises, and how long did you remain in your house in that period of three months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the morning the digging would begin at 6.00 a.m. And it would go on until late at night. Then they would take us to those premises, and if somebody needed a bath they would take him to his home under a military police escort. He would take a bath, spend the night, and in the morning they would take him to dig again at 6.00 a.m.. And this went on for about three months until they arranged those premises where we were, but we spent the least time in those premises because we were constantly out in the field with the soldiers and we would spend even up to a month sleeping in dug-outs and in tents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. This really -- the question is asked to test your credibility. And it seems to me, Mr. Sachdeva, that there was a problem in the translation. That's how it appears to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, with respect, I understand that the -- the sentence [B/C/S spoken] has been translated correctly in the English; in other words, he stayed home for three months. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Sachdeva is insisting on only the first three words: "I spent three months at home," but let the witness read the whole sentence and the previous text. So let him read not only the words Mr. Sachdeva is insisting on "I spent" -- but let him read everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not leave it except when I went to report, and then I returned again immediately under the escort with the Green Berets, and they came to search my house and they took away a lot of my things, a lot of my property, they looted it. I didn't say that here. It says here quite clearly that the military police brought me to take a bath. I wasn't allowed to leave the house. They would come to get me and take me away again, and this went on for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, it's correct, though, that you were not detained in a camp from April 1992 through to September 1994? You were not detained all of that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. From 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you, Witness, is that, as you have testified here today that you were in camp -- in a camp in Hrasnica from April 1992 through to September 1994, I'm suggesting to you that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Why is it not correct? If I was arrested on the 18th of April, 1992, and if they took us to our homes to have a bath and to have a shave and then they took us back and they took us to dig trenches every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. And I'm still going to stick with this statement you gave to the court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please. When you were at home, the Green Berets were controlling what you were doing. Were you able to get away at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would take us there and take us back again. No, no. Because there was a curfew and they were with us. We were not allowed to leave any positions, even when we were digging in the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't get the translation in French. I apologise. Could you repeat your answer, Witness, please, so that I can hear the translation. Witness, please, the -- I asked you this question to try to understand this apparent contradiction between your written statement and what you have said to us. This is why I am asking you this question. During the time you were at home at night, for instance, could you possibly get away, run away, and not go back; or were you always controlled by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't run away, because they were always present. They knew of each and every one of us when we were taken home to have a bath, and we were not allowed to leave until 6.00 a.m. the next morning, when they would come back to pick us up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So from April until September, you were, in fact, under arrest but you were at home, under house arrest. And during the day you were working for the armed forces of the ABiH to go and do your work. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You have the floor, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can take this issue any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, I now would like to, again, stay with this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 2 of the B/C/S version, also page -- and it's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But while we're trying to get there, Mr. Dukic, you were taken to the -- you said that you were taken to the Famos football stadium in -- on the 18th of April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said in your evidence that -- to the Court that you spent two or three hours there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then after the few hours that you were there, you said that you were taken to Aleksa Santic primary school. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: We were returned from the primary school to the stadium and then back to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In the premises, some stayed for seven days, while others returned to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking about you. Counsel for the Defence asked you: How long did you stay there, that is, the football stadium? And your answer was: "We spent only a few hours there."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Seven days. I may have misspoken, but I was there for seven days in the premises of the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And after you -- after you were at the football stadium, you were taken to the Aleksa Santic school. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Amir Sabovic met us there. I mentioned him. He knew all of us because he had worked at Famos and was later appointed a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were there for six days, five to six days, that's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes -- where five or six days?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At the primary school.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In the -- in the statement you gave to the court in Banja Luka at the -- if you see the page on your screen --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It says at the bottom that you spent 14 days at the school in Hrasnica, not six days. Which one is right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: As I said today, the stadium and the primary school of Aleksa Santic, the total of 14 days more or less. And then we were moved to the basement that they made. These rooms used to be a basement and they converted into rooms for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's your evidence that Mr. Ratko Stjepanovic was shot in the primary school. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Ratko Stjepanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you saw him shot? Did you see him being shot?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Because I used to know him well. He used to work with me in Famos, and all of us there knew him. We knew each other very well, all of us. Hrasnica is a small town and we all used to work in Famos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it, therefore, you would not confuse him -- you would not confuse his name, would you, you knew him well, as you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you look at the statement you gave in Banja Luka in March 1995, the name on the statement is Gojko Stjepanovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: As I said today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, today you said Ratko Stjepanovic, so which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, Gojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this is the person that you knew well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, it's correct, is it not, that in March 1994 you met someone called Mirko Pejanovic at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to mention that here today. I was taken to the Serbian citizens' council, and I met Mirko Pejanovic there as well as Jubomir Berberovic, Ejub Ganic, and a journalist of this -- Sarajevo radio, a woman by the name of Paunovic and others. I reported on the situation in Hrasnica, the situation with the Serbs, and Mr. Pejanovic and Berberovic reacted to it and after they came to visit Hrasnica, whereupon they saw the 96 graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that while you were meeting with the Serb representatives in Sarajevo that you were still detained, is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: When I was taken away from Hrasnica, taken through the tunnel to the Holiday Inn, to meet the people at the meeting of the Serbian Citizens' Council, I told Mr. Pejanovic about the things that were going on in Hrasnica and that we were actually being held in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's why I'm asking you that you were given an opportunity to represent the situation as you saw it with the Serbs in Hrasnica to a Serb representative at the Assembly and you also spoke to a journalist. And I'm asking you that in that situation are you still maintaining that you were detained?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, let's move on. You told the Court that you were taken to the trenches and you spoke about mortars. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your evidence was that there was fighting between the two belligerents at that location, on Mount Igman, I understand?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you can confirm that when you were speaking about mortars you were not talking about mortars in Hrasnica, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No, at Igman --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right, I just wanted to confirm that --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: -- but to me it is all Hrasnica. It is understood. Igman is not a locality, but it is a part of Hrasnica. Hrasnica is at the foot of Mount Igman. Half of the hills are actually on a slope -- half of the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But at the floor or at the base of Mount Igman where Hrasnica lies, it's a residential area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the mortars that you're talking about were on the slopes of Mount Igman. That's also right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the centre of Hrasnica, the residential area, civilians lived there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me that not only in Hrasnica but also in the centre of Sarajevo civilians lived there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in fact, as you have given evidence today, the civilians in Sarajevo comprised not just Muslim civilians, but also Serb civilians, Croat civilians, civilians of all ethnicities remained in Sarajevo, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, that the hardship that the civilians suffered in Sarajevo, the shelling of the city, the sniping into the city, not just Muslims suffered but also Serbs and Croats, they all suffered, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs were also were also targeted, were also sniped at, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: What sniping activity do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the full period from 1992 to 1995, and in particular 1994 to 1995, the VRS that were -- that encircled Sarajevo, you would agree that when they sniped into the city and sniped at civilians, it didn't matter to them whether the civilians were Muslim or Croat or Serb; everyone suffered, civilians suffered, and civilians of all ethnicities were targeted. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Since we had no electricity and could not follow the media, I don't know that. As for the suffering, any human being of any race, colour, or religious conviction suffers the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But in your time in Sarajevo, you knew that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were firing shells into the city, you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I did not even know of any Romanija Corps. I didn't know the establishment and units of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to talk to me about the organisation of the Romanija Corps. I'm simply asking you this: That in Sarajevo you knew that shells were being fired into the city in Sarajevo, you knew that, you heard about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I saw it happen on both sides. I saw shells being fired from one side and from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you knew that shells were being fired from the other side, that is, the VRS side into the city. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I could have only assumed or guessed at that. I didn't know it for a fact. You can't see Sarajevo from Hrasnica, you can see Ilidza and Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know when you say that you saw shells being fired from both sides, one side to another, you know that the shells that were fired on Sarajevo injured and killed civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know, as you have been -- as has been your role since you were released, you know that civilians are not supposed to be the object of attack, they are not supposed to suffer in war, are they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your time in Hrasnica, you heard about modified air-bombs being fired into the city -- into that residential area, as you've just testified about the area being residential?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it, and I didn't have such an experience with any air-bombs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did the witness testify to that? It was interpreted to us that the witness actually testified about knowing something about the air-bombs. I'm asking where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was: "In your time you heard about modified air-bombs being fired into the city," and, "into that residential area, as you have just testified about the area being residential." So the reference to testimony was about the area being residential not that he had testified about the air-bombs. What's your answer to that, Witness? Did you hear when you were in Hrasnica about modified air-bombs being fired into the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what a modified air-bomb is; although I served in the military. As for aviation we, didn't see any sorties in Hrasnica. As far as I know, there was no flying permitted let alone dropping bombs. As for the modified air-bombs, well, could someone please explain to me what it is and maybe then I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's fine, whether it was a modified air-bomb or mortar or other heavy weapons, you would agree with this proposition that the centre of Hrasnica would not be considered a military target and that it would be inappropriate to send shells into that town. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I have a second to confer with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour, I just would like to tender the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will go in as P773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to the question asked to you by the Prosecutor on page 63, line 20, to the question of whether you knew about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, you answered that you didn't know about it. Either about the corps or about any of these units. I would like to make sure that I understood you correctly; because you, as a reserve lieutenant who in addition you were indicted for dodging your call to serve under ABiH, you are saying that you didn't know that there was a -- an army corps called the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps which was there to detain the Serbian population -- or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To protect the Serbian population in Sarajevo. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've only learned of that in 1995 after I was released, it was then that I learned of any corps on the Serbian and the Bosnian side. I didn't have any access to information. I only know what was in Hrasnica. I know that there was the 4th motorised brigade there commanded by Fikret Prevljak. That is all. As for shells, they landed in, Sarajevo, Ilidza, Vojnici, Hrasnica, and so on and so forth. One could see that. We could also see a part of Dobrinja, Butmir, Ilidza, Hrasnica, Vojkovici, and Lukavica. That is what you can see from Hrasnica. As for the other parts of Sarajevo, Grbavica, Novi Grad, Stari Grad, and the rest, I couldn't see those because of the layout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Now, your situation was the following: You didn't know about any of the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Many Serbs in your situation didn't know about the activities or even the existence of this army corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about it until 1994, or rather, in 1995, after my exchange. On the 20th of January, 1995, it was then that I learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic? And how long will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not long, I think, a few questions concerning the statement that was tendered and a couple of extra questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were going to re-examine, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a number of questions concerning the statement of the 1st of March, 1995, that was tendered as a Prosecution exhibit. It used to be a 60 ter document which became the last Prosecutor's exhibit. The statement of the 1st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I can assist, I understand it's Exhibit P773.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please have a look at the date when you gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It should be notes on the questioning of a witness. Can you see the date? At the beginning. Witness, can you confirm to me what the date is on the document? Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The one you have in front of you "Record of Witness Interview." What date is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The 1st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when it was that you were released from the camp in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How heavy were you that day, compared to your regular weight?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I had 57 kilos upon my release, whereas I was 81 kilos heavy before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Famos factory that you used to work in before the conflict and before you were arrested, can you tell us where Famos was when the war broke out in relation to the two belligerent parties?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Half of it was dug into a hill since it was a military company, whereas the other half was on a clearing. Outside -- immediately outside the perimeter there was a Serb settlement called Vojkovici, and then what follows is Krupac, Kotorac, Lukavica, and so on. Looking at the other gate to the factory, Hrasnica was there and that part was in no man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Towards Vojkovici, and towards Trnovo at Igman, towards the source of the Bosna, and I said that there was Tito's villa there at Stojcevac, and then towards Ilidza past the soccer club of Igman, and then towards Butmir and the tunnel. That is the area where I was digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were doing there what type of military operations on either side were you able to observe, as you were frequently there on the spot digging trenches, so what could you see from there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, first I'll tell you that on the Serb side there were infantry weapons and artillery weapons. On the Muslim side there were also infantry weapons and artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons firing on Serb positions, where did whatever they fired land?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, from Igman they were firing on Ilidza, Kotorac, Lukavica, Vojkovici, and Trnovo. I don't know where the positions were on the other side, but shells came from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the tunnel you worked on and you've told us enough about it, but can you tell me whether any troops moved through the area where you were digging?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the tunnel was built in order to establish communication between Sarajevo via Igman, Lokve, above Hadzici and Bradina to Mostar. That was the line that they -- the route they moved along. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, leave him aside, I'm not interested in that. But please tell us, did you notice where the command post of this brigade was that Fikret Prevljak was commanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In the post office in Hrasnica, in the basement of the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, where is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the centre of the town, the post office, and the command was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When answering questions put by my learned friend, you spoke about how Sarajevo was targeted. Was Grbavica part of Sarajevo? Nedzarici, was Nedzarici part of Sarajevo? What is Sarajevo, explain to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see whether there was any firing from Grbavica or Nedzarici or the other places, but Sarajevo consists of Vogosca, Ilijas, below Pale, Trnovo, Hadzici, and over there by way of Ilidza. All that was the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you what Grbavica is. Is that Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Sarajevo, too, that's the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No, the settlement of Nedzarici is closer to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nedzarici are not part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are, it is, but geographically it's closer to Ilidza, but Ilidza is also part of Sarajevo. It's all part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you finished what you were doing in Hrasnica, you were taken to Viktor Bubanj. Did you see anything from there, what was happening outside?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: No, because I was in cell number 1 so I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, now, in my submission, this moves beyond the cross-examination. In fact, my learned friend had asked the witness questions about the Viktor Bubanj barracks in chief, and in my submission that would have been the appropriate time to ask these follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel says this doesn't arise from his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva asked directly, as is his right, whether he saw civilians being killed in Sarajevo, and I am asking, in view of the fact that he was where he was in Sarajevo what he was able to see from there. Because civilians were killed on both sides, as was said here, and my question is what he was able to see from his prison cell at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't see anything from the Viktor Bubanj barracks because I was in cell number 1, and I couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take a look at what's on the record here and finish this. Let's look at page 3 in B/C/S. I don't know where it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 3 shown to the witness, the paragraph before the last.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this what you said when you were describing how you were digging trenches and what happened then? If we look at page 3, is that what you said then?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I can't see. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It starts: "November 1992 ..." It's the second paragraph in English, and if you look at the passage in B/C/S, towards the end of the passage, it says: "Every Serb ..." and please tell me whether this corresponds to what you have been saying here.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I can't see very well. I do apologise, but I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see it very well. They're now showing it to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: "Every Serb" -- you mean "we who were digging 2 and a half metres, 140 centimetres deep, and 90 centimetres wide," that's the trenches that the two of us had to dig in one day, that was the norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: We were mistreated and beaten. I didn't say that because I was trying to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please read what it says here, read how you buried people.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that I tendered this statement; however, I tendered this statement purely on the issue of credibility on the apparent contradiction between whether the witness was detained or whether the witness could -- was free to go to his house. These questions, in my submission, should have been asked in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Don't ask any more questions about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Tapuskovic, to another question. Let's finish this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will finish, but this is a statement I have not seen before. It was introduced by the Prosecution. It has to do allegedly with the credibility of this witness which has been challenged, but these are matters which can confirm his credibility by showing what he experienced. This document can demonstrate the witness's credibility in view of what he said a month after he left prison with half the weight he had when he entered it. If I can only put one more passage to him so that the entire statement can be considered with respect to the witness's credibility. Because if his credibility is being challenged, let him say who all the people were who were killed and how many people were killed with their first and last names, because he remembered that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if the question that you are going to put relates to the credibility of the witness and if it relates to the -- to the issue raised by Mr. Sachdeva, yes, you can put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not be obstinate. This document is in evidence. I will ask a question put by Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Pejanovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: You're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic and Mrs. Lujic were in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they loyal citizens?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: They were loyal citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened, you were taken from prison, where?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: To the Serb Citizens' Council, and I told Mr. Pejanovic on that occasion what we Serbs were doing and how we were being maltreated in Hrasnica. After that he visited Hrasnica. He saw for himself that there were 96 graves there, and then he sent Mr. Ljubomir Berberovic, an academician.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you were sent back to prison?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: We had already been taken back to prison through the same tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic, that is your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not prepared that list. May we go into closed -- private session. Just a moment, please, to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were born on the 5th of January, 1940?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Nevesinje in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've been living in Sarajevo since 1955?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo you completed secondary school and the faculty for physical education?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, all of that data should be in private session, Mr. Waespi, or it doesn't matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, it's up to the witness. Since he said his name shouldn't be made public, I think all these other identifying features should also not be made public, but that's just my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I explained all this to the witness, and all the witness is asking is that his first and last name not be pronounced, not be mentioned. He doesn't want to protect any other piece of information, that's the witness's decision, which I respect. As it's the witness's wish, I think it's all permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As long as he understands that by the personal data being given, his -- it is possible for somebody to identify him and to -- but if he understands that and he's perfectly prepared to go along with it, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I'm doing all this because of my wife and children in Sarajevo. I speak in public about the things I will testify about. I have even written a book about them, so there's no reason for me to conceal anything and to expedite matters and to speed things up, I decided that we needn't move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have a Ph.D. in that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the -- you've been working at the Faculty of Physical Education since then?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Since before the war in Sarajevo, and in the wartime conditions I became the dean of the faculty for sports in Serbian Sarajevo, and I still work there as a professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just for the last time to make the point. I think it's clear to everybody in Sarajevo, even I'm not from Sarajevo, that this gentleman was the dean of the faculty of sports, even if the name isn't mentioned, that's clear. So it just seems to me -- odd for me, but it's the last time I'm making this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you understand that these personal data will allow somebody to identify you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not afraid of my testimony or ashamed of it. I wrote a book, I have written in the newspapers, I'm such a public personage that it doesn't bother me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a long discussion with the witness about this, and it's his decision so I don't see why I should oppose it because the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, for the sake of brevity, as you said that you'd written a book, you testified in another case - you don't have to mention where. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you very briefly explain to Their Honours what happened in Sarajevo in 1992 and in what circumstances you remained in the part of Sarajevo under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The events in Sarajevo, and especially the events in the old town and the area of Bistrik where I resided, were the forerunners of all the events that would ensue. Why was Bistrik and the old town the epicentre of everything that happened precisely because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. In order to make this completely clear to Their Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a map on the monitor. It's 65 ter 2872. If this eastern part could be enlarged and put in the middle of the monitor, please. A little more, if possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now show Their Honours where the place where you lived in is. You said it was at Bistrik?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's this position here. It's red, this red area. I think it's a park.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with the letter K?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if this thing would write. That's the old town and Bistrik where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please mark this with a K.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: [Marks] -- Oh, like this. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened here in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I said this was the epicentre of everything that was to follow in wartime Sarajevo. Why do I say this? Well, precisely because this part of the old town was more than 90 per cent Muslim or Bosniak, as they say now, according to ethnic make-up. And there was a military command there, the Supreme Command of General Kukanjac was there in the old town. There was already hostility towards soldiers of the JNA. People no longer saw those soldiers as soldiers of the people; they saw them as unwanted, undesirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we don't have much time, so please tell us only what is essential.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I'd be happy to. At that time in early 1992, say in February, March, and April, we could see people wearing the uniforms of the Green Berets with a patch sporting a lily emblem, and that emblem was to become the emblem of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I could see military vehicles with mounted machine-guns and soldiers sporting handguns, rifles, rifle-launched grenades. I saw all these war models, so to say, carrying knives and stuff -- well, everything that can be found in any war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was happening with you and your family?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: All that contributed to an atmosphere in which the people had to decide whether to stay or to leave. Most people decided to take their families out of the city, the elderly and children, and they -- most of them left on the planes to Belgrade as well as towards the embassies in Croatia, particularly in Split. My children went to Split to stay with my wife's parents. My wife and I stayed in Sarajevo, since after the 15th of May one could no longer leave the city. It was encircled from all sides, all roads and intersections around the road saw check-points being established manned by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police and no one could leave legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said "around the city"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: There were trenches being dug around the city and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took up positions there with weaponry. It was understandable that no one dared to approach or -- and try to leave the city via such positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us more about the -- these positions that were taken up by the ABiH around the city. Exactly what does that mean, around the city? How far -- for example, how far were these positions apart from each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that for the two years in the wartime Sarajevo until I left, I was digging trenches and I know the situation very well. Perhaps I can mark it on the map. They were up on the hills of Trebevic and on the north-eastern side at Borije hill. The distance was 20, 50, up to 100 metres between the trenches. And down below here where the trenches were engineered at the Jewish cemetery at Nedzarici, the distance was perhaps one block of flats or one wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how did it come about? You were providing an answer posed by the President. How did it come about that you started performing such work?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, there were two drafts in Sarajevo. The one carried out by the Croat authorities for their population between the ages of 16 and 65, they were enlisted with the HVO. And their premises were in certain schools where they were quartered. Another draft was for the Muslims and the Serbs and others, which took place in another location. We were all sent draft calls despite any previous limitation that had been set as to our physical ability. I was included in a special forces unit, although I indicated that I had back problems and that I had not served with the JNA and that I had no military experience. Still, they put me in a special forces unit. I never reported to the unit, I never wanted to take up arms; therefore, I spent the rest of my time digging trenches for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How old were you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show the Judges on this map where it was that you were digging trenches. Perhaps you can mark all those locations with a -- with short lines.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Let's start from here. This is the road to Pale and to the Olympic centre at Jahorina. We were digging at the Ablakovina part around here, whereas the Serb forces were down below on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Here, and the Serb forces were on the road. That was the distance. I think it was less than 30 metres here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where else?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: These are the slopes of Mount Trebevic. This is below the funicular. There were Muslim forces there and below there were the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark each of the locations.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Here, Jarcev Dol, and there is a hill here, and we had to dig there during the night, not to be seen. Then across the Miljacka and on the slopes here called Borije, and then we dug high up here. I don't think it's on the map, it's called Donje Divosko, we were digging here. If you have the photographs here, perhaps we can show it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: This is the position, and further up the hill. It is about an hour's walk from the urban part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did it look like? How long would you stay each time to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, we were all collected from the streets. And Moso Topalovic, Caco, who commanded the 10th Mountain Brigade he encircled the entire area, and they picked up everyone who was able to do anything. We were taken up there to dig trenches, which also presented an obstacle to the proper functioning of the city; because people used to work in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you were collected in the street, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: It was an attack. They took up positions on both sides of the street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have an indication of the time-frame because that will speed up cross-examination if we can figure out when all these digging of trenches happened. If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was just told by my colleague it is 1992, but I don't know whether the witness gave that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less between June -- well, and for a month or two until they reined in Caco, the commander, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. And the rest of the time was spent digging trenches, although they treated us better. Although the actual practice of picking people up from the street never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when did that last?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: I left in June 1994, although I know that some people stayed behind, and they were forced to keep on digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's look at DD003790. Excuse me, let us save the map with its markings, and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show DD003790 to the witness. Could we enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the date and what is stated below the heading.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: The date is the 3rd of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Read the next part out loud. You've referred to it before, or rather, it should show -- and tell us about the things you mentioned. Perhaps you can tell us what is mentioned here in the order.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "Committee for the establishment of responsibility with regard to inhabitants of Sarajevo being taken to preform engineering works." And what follows is: "Order" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: "Based on official requests from a large number of citizens, several institutions in the town of Sarajevo committee -- court," and: "Order," strictly confidential number stated, "which was not put into practice and with a view of determining what the situation is concerning the unlawful detaining and taking away of a number of citizens of Sarajevo to perform engineering work at the front lines" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this tally with what was taking place in the city?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. It says here, "Considering the continuing practice of forcible removal and taking away of citizens." Although there were calls from the municipality to report in a certain place which was a much more pleasant practice, people were still collected in various ways. As soon as they would realise that they were not with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or that they had no work obligation, people would be taken away to dig trenches. And it is what this document is about, I presume. Citizens did intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at page 2 to see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sefer Halilovic, Supreme Command Staff, yes, Sefer was the chief of the ABiH Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, DD00379, I wish to tender it as a Defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction 3790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for the record this is the first time we've seen this. I've just checked, it's been communicated to us, I think, an hour ago, just to put it on the record but just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An hour is all of 60 minutes. Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this document from the Office of the Prosecutor not long ago, on Friday. Your Honours, I now wish to show a photograph DD003969. If it could be brought up on the screen. It's in e-court. I showed it to the Prosecutor, to my learned friend Mr. Waespi, and as I understand it he does not object to having this photograph shown to the Court and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what does this show? What street is this?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: This is Bistricka Street in the area where I resided and where the 10th Mountain Brigade of Topalovic Caco was active. On the right-hand side one can see the headquarters of Commander Topalovic, and a few metres away from it is the military command where the Egyptian battalion was later to take up residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this your street?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the street where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show the places on this photograph where you dug trenches, if you can mark that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We dug trenches behind those rocks about a bit deeper in, and there's a road there taking -- leading to the Olympic village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But please listen to me. Compared to this ridge, where were you digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Below the ridge and behind this rock. That's Ablakovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On which side of the rock were you digging -- or the ridge, rather?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: From this side of the ridge, some 50 metres in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to explain clearly, this side, that side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Behind, behind this rock, some 50 metres behind this rock, there's a meadow there and that's where we dug. And 40 metres beyond the meadow is a road where the Serb forces were. I think I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of this ridge?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Ablakovina. I found out about these names when I was digging trenches. I didn't know what these places were called before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you show us where the Serb forces were. You said 40 metres beyond the meadow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beyond the meadow on the road leading to Pale or the Jahorina Olympic centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you mark it with a little X?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Behind this here, if I can draw a line between these rocks and the hill up there, that's where the road went, 50 metres behind the rocks, so you can't see it here. These are the foothills of Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So who was at the higher point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one can't really say who was higher than the other side because we kind of looked at each other eye to eye. It was on the same level. Everywhere else, if you go to the right of Borije, it was the Serb forces that held the higher ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: All right, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness is not angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Redact it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As long as it doesn't get into the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Robinson put a good question to you. Can you say who was holding the higher ground here if you look at it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this whole road leading up there, the Serb forces were there, and they were some 50 or 20 metres away from each other. That's how it was. We could see each other. We looked at each other. Along this whole road leading up to Trebevic it would be hard to say who was holding the higher ground. They were right next to each other, because if I can tell you the strategy of the fighting was similar to that in sport, you know, when there is a clinch. You are thinking of victory, so the closer I am, the stronger I'll be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Leave sports aside now. Just tell us who was holding the foothills on that last bend, that last mountain pass.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Which mountain pass?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't testify. Just tell us. You said that the forces were close to each other, and who was holding that point? You can see on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, where is the funicular?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, there isn't a funicular there. That's not that picture --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness answered, he said, you know, we were also at the same level. I also remind you, Mr. President, this witness left the situation on the 9th of June, 1994, so he doesn't really assist to the indictment period as it relates to this part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He may answer the question. But bear in mind that he's actually your witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Witness, before testifying here, you know how things work here. The ridge that you marked here, you marked with a single line. The single line shows both the trenches you dug and the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, as you say. Can you separate this. You've already said it's behind the ridge. So can you now draw the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska because you drew a single line?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have to draw a parallel line here on the same level, and those would be the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, behind this line. But they were on the same level, so you couldn't see that line from where we are looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our time is up, so could we just save this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be saved, and we'll resume tomorrow at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of June, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
